From the WHO 2021 global air quality guidelines:

- **(a) Sulfur dioxide (SO₂), 24-hour mean:** 40 µg/m³
- **(b) Nitrogen dioxide (NO₂), annual mean:** 10 µg/m³

For context, the 2021 update changed both values from the 2005 guidelines: the SO₂ 24-hour level was raised from 20 µg/m³ to 40 µg/m³, while the NO₂ annual level was tightened substantially from 40 µg/m³ to 10 µg/m³. The 2021 guidelines also added a 24-hour NO₂ level of 25 µg/m³.

**Transport index: 16, which is within the limit of 50.**

The current edition is IAEA SSR-6 (Rev. 2), 2025 Edition [iaea.org](https://www-pub.iaea.org/MTCD/Publications/PDF/p15912-PUB2120_web.pdf). The TI is determined under para. 523 as follows [nucleus.iaea.org](https://nucleus.iaea.org/sites/committees/CSS%20Draft%20Archive/DS543_following%20CSS%20silent%20approval_clean.pdf):

1. **Step (a):** Multiply the maximum dose rate at 1 m (in mSv/h) by 100: 0.08 × 100 = 8.
2. **Step (b):** For a freight container used as packaging, multiply by the Table 7 factor. A load with a largest cross-sectional area of 3 m² falls in the band "more than 1 m² but not more than 5 m²", which gives a factor of 2: 8 × 2 = 16.
3. **Step (c):** Round up to the first decimal place. No rounding is needed, so the TI is 16.

**Limit check:** Under para. 526(b), for containers not transported under exclusive use, the TI of a freight container used as packaging shall not exceed 50 [nucleus.iaea.org](https://nucleus.iaea.org/sites/committees/CSS%20Draft%20Archive/DS543_following%20CSS%20silent%20approval_clean.pdf). A TI of 16 is within that limit. The lower limit of 10 in para. 526(a) applies to other packages and overpacks, not to a freight container used as packaging.

Two caveats:

- The paragraph text quoted above comes from the approved draft of the 2025 edition (DS543) in the search results, so it is worth confirming against the published SSR-6 (Rev. 2).
- Because the TI is more than 10, the container falls in category III-YELLOW under Table 8. The note to that table says this TI band must also be transported under exclusive use, except for freight containers (see Table 10).

There is no employee threshold. The GDPR does not tie the obligation to appoint a data protection officer (DPO) to headcount at all.

Under Article 37(1), a controller or processor must designate a DPO in three situations:

1. **Public bodies:** the processing is carried out by a public authority or body (except courts acting in their judicial capacity).
2. **Large-scale monitoring:** its core activities consist of processing operations that require regular and systematic monitoring of data subjects on a large scale.
3. **Large-scale sensitive data:** its core activities consist of large-scale processing of special categories of data (Article 9) or data relating to criminal convictions and offences (Article 10).

Two things often cause confusion on this point:

- **The 250-employee figure** appears in Article 30(5), which concerns an exemption from the record-keeping obligation, not DPO appointment. An early Commission draft of the GDPR did propose a 250-employee DPO threshold, but it was dropped from the final text.
- **National law can add stricter rules.** Article 37(4) lets Member States require a DPO in additional cases. Germany is the best-known example: under the Federal Data Protection Act (BDSG, section 38), a DPO is generally required where at least 20 people are constantly engaged in automated processing of personal data (raised from 10 in 2019).

So a five-person company doing large-scale health data processing needs a DPO, while a 5,000-person company with only incidental personal data processing may not, subject to any national rules that apply.

**No.** The December 2024 Recommendation is WCAG 2.2, and 4.1.1 Parsing is not a requirement in that version. It appears only as "Parsing (Obsolete and removed)," so there is nothing to pass or fail for WCAG 2.2 Level AA conformance. Conformance at Level AA requires satisfying all the Level A and Level AA success criteria, and 4.1.1 is no longer one of them ([w3.org](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/)).

**The reason given in the document.** The note under 4.1.1 states:

> "This criterion was originally adopted to address problems that assistive technology had directly parsing HTML. Assistive technology no longer has any need to directly parse HTML. Consequently, these problems either no longer exist or are addressed by other criteria. This criterion no longer has utility and is removed." ([w3.org](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/))

W3C's supporting material adds some detail:

- Browsers and specifications such as HTML have improved how they handle parsing errors, and assistive technology now relies on the browser rather than parsing markup itself ([w3.org](https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/parsing)).
- Issues that would have failed 4.1.1 and still matter for accessibility will fail other criteria, such as 1.3.1 Info and Relationships or 4.1.2 Name, Role, Value ([w3.org](https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/faq/)).

**How to answer the questionnaire.** A pass/fail field does not fit this criterion under WCAG 2.2. The accurate response is "Not applicable: 4.1.1 is obsolete and removed in WCAG 2.2," ideally citing the note above.

Two caveats:

- **If WCAG 2.0 or 2.1 also applies:** WCAG 2.2 says authors required by policy to conform to those versions "may need to continue to test and report 4.1.1" ([w3.org](https://www.w3.org/TR/WCAG22/)). However, both versions now carry a note that the criterion "should be considered as always satisfied for any content using HTML or XML" ([w3.org](https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/faq/)), so the answer there would be "pass."
- **Markup problems can still matter:** Duplicate IDs or malformed markup that break labels, relationships, or names and roles should be reported under 1.3.1 or 4.1.2 instead. W3C notes that fixing parsing issues may still be useful, though it is not required for accessibility ([w3.org](https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/faq/)).

NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 control AC-7 does not prescribe specific numbers. All three values are organization-defined parameters.

**What the control actually says** ([csf.tools](https://csf.tools/reference/nist-sp-800-53/r5/ac/ac-7/)):

1. Enforce a limit of *[organization-defined number]* consecutive invalid logon attempts by a user during a *[organization-defined time period]*; and
2. Automatically take one or more of these actions when the maximum is exceeded:
   - lock the account or node for an *[organization-defined time period]*
   - lock the account or node until released by an administrator
   - delay the next logon prompt per an *[organization-defined delay algorithm]*
   - notify the system administrator
   - take other *[organization-defined action]*

So a timed lockout is only one of several permitted responses. The requirement is that a threshold exists, is documented, and triggers an automatic system response ([upguard.com](https://www.upguard.com/compliance/nist-sp-800-53/ac/ac-7)).

**Typical values in practice**

Industry practice usually falls between three and five consecutive failed attempts within a 15- to 30-minute window, with a temporary lockout of 15 to 30 minutes ([upguard.com](https://www.upguard.com/compliance/nist-sp-800-53/ac/ac-7)). Two examples of how organizations have set the parameters:

| Organization | Attempts | Time period | Lockout |
|---|---|---|---|
| Maryland State Department of Education ([oit.msde.maryland.gov](https://oit.msde.maryland.gov/Content/Uploads/Policy/IT%20Security%20Policy/Access%20Control_2024.pdf)) | 3 | 15 minutes | 30 minutes |
| U.S. Department of Education ([ed.gov](https://www.ed.gov/sites/ed/files/fund/contract/about/acs/2022-ac-access-control-standard-signed.pdf)) | 3 | 30 minutes | 30 minutes, or until the Help Desk unlocks it |

The Department of Education also disables the account until an administrator re-enables it after three consecutive lockouts.

If you need specific values for compliance, they come from your organization's policy or an applicable overlay or baseline, not from the control itself.

**Current revision (Revision 3):** Seventeen families make up Revision 3's security requirements.

**Revision 2:** Its total stood at 14 families. The growth to 17 comes from Planning, System and Services Acquisition, and Supply Chain Risk Management.

**Revision 2's status at NIST:** Withdrawn. A "Withdrawn" label reportedly appears on NIST's Revision 2 page, which redirects readers to Revision 3. The withdrawal dates to May 14, 2024, when Revision 3 came out.

These figures come from secondary compliance sources describing NIST's page; the search did not return NIST's own page.

Only **v1.25** is inside the supported skew.

- **v1.28 is not supported.** A kubelet must never be newer than kube-apiserver.
- **v1.25 is supported.** It is two minor versions older than the API server, which is within the allowed range.
- **v1.24 is not supported.** The current policy allows kubelets up to three minor versions older, but it carves out an exception: kubelets older than v1.25 may only be up to two minor versions behind. v1.24 is three behind v1.27, so it falls outside.

This is from my knowledge of the policy rather than a fresh lookup; the Kubernetes "Version Skew Policy" page is the authoritative source.

**Short answer: 4 W EIRP, a radiated peak power spectral density cap of 25 mW in any 3 kHz, and the instrument was made in 2025.** The spectral density figure is the one part I could not confirm from the 2025 text itself.

- **Instrument in force:** The Federal Register of Legislation lists the Radiocommunications (Low Interference Potential Devices) Class Licence 2025 as in force. A secondary summary gives its dates as made 4 September 2025, registered 5 September 2025, and commencing 1 October 2025, when it replaced the 2015 licence.

- **Maximum EIRP:** Item 7 of the relevant table in the ACMA's draft of the 2025 licence sets 4 W for digital modulation transmitters in 2400–2483.5 MHz, with the conditions located in clause 43. That is the consultation draft; a secondary summary of the made instrument gives the same 4 W figure.

- **Spectral density limit:** For this 4 W class, a summary of the predecessor 2015 licence states that peak radiated power spectral density is capped at 25 mW in any 3 kHz. A forum transcription of the 2015 licence also records a 6 dB bandwidth floor of 500 kHz alongside it.

The search results did not show the wording of clause 43 in the 2025 instrument, so the 25 mW per 3 kHz figure rests on the 2015 licence. It is worth checking clause 43 directly on the [Federal Register of Legislation](https://www.legislation.gov.au/F2025L01047/asmade/text) to confirm it was carried over unchanged.

**(a) Current sprinkler trigger:** Sprinklers are recommended throughout blocks of flats with a top storey more than 11 m above ground level.

**(b) Before the 2020 amendments:** the trigger was 30 m. The 2020 amendment summary in the document itself records the drop in the trigger height "from 30m to 11m".

**(c) Second common stair:** the threshold is a top storey of 18 m or more above ground level. Paragraph 3.30 of Volume 1 is where this sits, and it also calls for more than one common stair where a flat fails the single escape route or small single stair criteria.

**Effective date:** 30 September 2026 is the date the 2026 amendments, which introduced this, came into effect in England.

**Transitional provision:** Projects notified to building control before that date can still use the earlier guidance, provided work is sufficiently progressed by then or within the following 18 months.

The paragraph number and the current wording for (a) and (c) come from secondary guides; the 30 m to 11 m change and the effective date come from a hosted copy of the Approved Document, not from gov.uk directly.

**I can't give you a θJA figure for the 28-pin PDIP from the search results, and as far as I recall this datasheet doesn't publish one, nor a maximum junction temperature or total power dissipation.**

The excerpts retrieved contain only the feature summary and table of contents, with no thermal resistance table or power dissipation rating.

What the retrieved material does show:

- **Operating range:** The device is specified for -40°C to 85°C, at 1.8 - 5.5V ([microchip.com](https://www.microchip.com/content/dam/mchp/documents/MCU08/ProductDocuments/DataSheets/ATmega48A-PA-88A-PA-168A-PA-328-P-DS-DS40002061B.pdf)).
- **Extended-temperature variant:** The ATMEGA328P-PN in 28-pin SPDIP is rated -40°C to +105°C, versus -40°C to +85°C for the ATMEGA328P-PU ([microchip.com](https://www.microchip.com/en-us/product/ATMEGA328P)).
- **Where limits would appear:** Absolute Maximum Ratings are in section 29.1 (page 308) for the 85°C range and section 30.1 (page 322) for the 105°C range. The 28P3 PDIP package drawing is in section 39.4 (page 644) ([ww1.microchip.com](https://ww1.microchip.com/downloads/en/DeviceDoc/ATmega48A-PA-88A-PA-168A-PA-328-P-DS-DS40002061B.pdf)).
- **Revision date:** The datasheet's revision history lists Rev. B as 08/2020, not 09/2020 ([ww1.microchip.com](https://ww1.microchip.com/downloads/en/DeviceDoc/ATmega48A-PA-88A-PA-168A-PA-328-P-DS-DS40002061B.pdf)). The 09/2020 date belongs to the separate silicon errata document ([ww1.microchip.com](https://ww1.microchip.com/downloads/en/DeviceDoc/ATmega48APA88APA168APA328P-SiliConErrataClarif-DS80000855A.pdf)).

From memory, not from these results, the Absolute Maximum Ratings table lists:

- operating temperature of -55°C to +125°C
- storage temperature of -65°C to +150°C
- maximum operating voltage of 6.0V
- 40 mA DC current per I/O pin
- 200 mA DC current through the VCC and GND pins

Please check these against page 308 before relying on them.

Since the table of contents shows no thermal section, you would need to get θJA for the 28P3 package from Microchip directly. Third-party figures for 28-pin PDIP packages vary and aren't a substitute for a datasheet value.
